title: A name no one had heard
hookLine: the baby is named Muhammad, the praised one, in the Year of the Elephant

cards: Someone once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about fasting on Mondays. His answer, in Sahih Muslim: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation first came to me. So the story begins on a Monday, in Mecca.
The sirah places it in the Year of the Elephant, the year Abraha's army turned back. His father Abdullah, the ransomed son, has already died, the sirah says. His mother Amina holds the baby.
And his grandfather, Abd al-Muttalib, gives him a name. Today: Muhammad.

teach.b: The name is Muhammad. Tradition says it was rare among the Arabs then.
A story people tell says the grandfather was asked why he chose a name nobody in the family had, and answered that he hoped the boy would be praised in heaven and on earth.
That story comes from later books, so hold it lightly.
Tradition explains the name from the root h-m-d, praise, the root of al-hamdu lillah, praise belongs to Allah, the line the Fatiha opens with after the basmala.

In that telling, Muhammad means the one praised, and praised again: the much-praised. The Qur'an uses his name plainly. In surah forty-eight, Pickthall translates: "Muhammad is the messenger of Allah."

And it uses another form of the same root. In surah sixty-one, 'Isa, son of Maryam, gives good news of a messenger who will come after him, and Pickthall renders the name "the Praised One." The Arabic there is Ahmad.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet lists his own names, and Muhammad and Ahmad come first. Notice the shape of it. He is the praised one, but the root's first job, every time the Fatiha is recited, is praising Allah.
The praise in his name points beyond him. And there's a small, warm instruction in al-Bukhari, too.
Call yourselves by my name, he said.

teach.h: MUHAMMAD IS THE MESSENGER OF ALLAH.
teach.b: A name tradition calls rare back then is one you may well have heard today.

how: Muhammad and Ahmad are given as names in honor of the Prophet ﷺ, and some Muslims fast on Mondays, following his practice and remembering his birth.

o: the orphan, the one with no father
the messenger, the one who is sent
the much-praised, from the root of praise

games.q: a name no one had heard — tap the pairs.
p: the Praised One, in surah sixty-one
the day he said he was born

s: tradition explains Muhammad and Ahmad from the same root
h-m-d, praise, as in al-hamdu lillah.
the Prophet told people not to use his name
in al-Bukhari he says: call yourselves by my name.
it's certain why his grandfather chose the name
the story of his reason comes from later books; hold it lightly.

games.q: someone asks the Prophet ﷺ why he fasts on Mondays. what does he answer?
o: it's the day the Ka'ba was built.
it's the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
it's the day the elephant turned back.
games.why: Sahih Muslim reports it: the day he was born, and the day revelation first came to him.

practice: Say your own name silently, and ask whether you know what it means, or who chose it and why; if you do, hold the meaning a while, and if you don't, hold the not-knowing, and the person who chose it for you.
A name is often somebody's hope. If you pray, you can thank Allah for whoever named you; if you don't, let your name sound once more, gently, in your head.

wordCard.voice: Muhammad. The much-praised, from the root of praise, given by his grandfather, the sirah says, in the Year of the Elephant. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Muhammad; tradition explains it as the much-praised, from h-m-d, praise.

carryVoice: Your line: the praised one. Tomorrow, Halimah's thin donkey. That's day seven hundred six.
